title: Teaching
text:
I teach students to think scientifically and become increasingly independent by making complex work manageable, active, applied, and connected to goals beyond a single course. Across courses and research mentoring, my goal is to help students become careful consumers and producers of evidence.
I use scaffolding not to lower expectations, but to make high expectations attainable. Students practice component skills, receive feedback, and then apply that feedback in more independent work.

title: Teaching
text:
Courses Taught



PSY 250


Research Design & Analysis I

Instructor of record · Summer 2026 · Online asynchronous

I independently designed course materials, assignments, exams, lecture recordings, weekly learning activities, grading structures, and feedback systems, with support from two undergraduate teaching assistants.
The course centers research design, scientific writing, critical thinking, and transferable skills such as project management, analytic reasoning, problem solving, and communication.




PSY 317


Social Psychology Lab

Instructor of record · Fall 2024; Summers 2024-2026

PSY 317 is an upper-level seminar/lab course emphasizing replication, open science, research design, and scientific reasoning. Students engage with preregistration, questionable research practices, registered reports, publication bias, scientific disagreement, research design, and transparent scientific writing.




Additional Teaching Experience
My graduate teaching assistant experience includes PSY 250 Research Design and Analysis I, PSY 315 Social Psychology, and PSY 350 Research Design and Analysis II / Statistics. Guest teaching has included health psychology, attitudes and persuasion, independent and dependent variables, moderation and mediation, and article-based study design.

title: Teaching
text:
How I Teach


01

Build Independence Through Scaffolding
In PSY 250, the semester-long research proposal is broken into manageable stages: assignment orientation, article review, literature search, research idea, hypothesis and variables, outlines, peer review, full introduction, final proposal, and presentation.



02

Think Scientifically
Students compare popular or public-facing science claims with original research articles, asking whether causal language is appropriate, whether limitations were omitted, and whether conclusions go beyond the design.



03

Learn Actively
I use think-pair-share, small-group discussion, applied examples, reflection questions, discussion boards, group problem solving, student-generated examples, and research-design activities.



04

Structure Collaboration
Group work is designed around clear expectations, defined responsibilities, peer evaluation, and safeguards against free riding. In online summer courses, I continue to refine how collaboration can remain useful without adding unnecessary coordination burden.



05

Connect Learning To Transferable Skills
Students practice critical thinking, project management, teamwork, communication, public speaking, evidence evaluation, and scientific literacy. A student does not need to become a psychologist for these skills to matter.



06

Practice Reflective Improvement
I use student feedback to revise pacing, scaffolding, readings, online structure, assignment instructions, and accessibility of learning activities while preserving core learning goals.

Doctoral Candidate in Applied Social and Health Psychology
Colorado State University


I am a health-behavior scientist studying how health-promoting behaviors can be integrated into everyday life in ways that are feasible, sustainable, and minimally disruptive to the other demands people face. My work focuses especially on physical activity, sedentary behavior, workplace and everyday settings, intervention fit, and sustained behavior change.
Rather than asking whether an intervention works “on average” alone, I study when, for whom, and under what conditions interventions are usable, effective, and sustainable.

title: Mentoring
text:
Research assistants should leave with more than completed hours. Their time in the lab should produce skills, confidence, career clarity, and increasing independence.
I treat research mentoring as career development rather than assuming every undergraduate wants the same research career. Some students need research-intensive preparation for graduate school; others are exploring psychology, building professional skills, or learning what research work actually looks like.

title: Mentoring
text:
Developmental Model

01 Individualize 02 Build structure 03 Transfer autonomy 04 Create leadership opportunities


Individualize
At the beginning of a mentoring relationship, I learn why a student joined the lab, what they hope to build, how long they expect to stay, and whether they are interested in graduate school, research, clinical work, or another path.


Build Structure
New research assistants begin with detailed protocols, expectations for reliability and communication, mock sessions, documentation practices, research-ethics guidance, and close feedback.


Transfer Autonomy
As students gain skill, the question shifts from whether they can follow a procedure to whether they understand why it matters. Students increasingly troubleshoot, interpret articles, connect procedures to design logic, and contribute to project development.


Create Leadership Opportunities
Experienced students may take on peer training, recruitment coordination, data-quality roles, science communication, project management, conference dissemination, manuscript involvement, or project-specific leadership.
This model helps a large research team remain educational rather than purely logistical.

title: Mentoring
section: Weekly Lab Meeting As Research Seminar
text:
Weekly Lab Meeting As Research Seminar
Weekly lab meetings are a major educational component of the research experience. They often include protocol and deviation review, assigned article discussion, student-generated questions, mini-lessons, applied methods exercises, project updates, and scientific communication practice.
These meetings expose students to the research lifecycle: how an idea becomes a protocol, a dataset, an analysis, a presentation, and eventually a manuscript.

title: Mentoring
text:
Research Lifecycle Exposure
Depending on timing and interest, students may participate in idea development, literature searching, protocol writing, IRB preparation, recruitment, data collection, participant communication, data organization, analysis, poster preparation, conference presentation, manuscript writing, and publication.
Students who cannot participate in every stage still learn about those stages through lab meetings and project updates.

title: Mentoring
text:
Career Development
Research-oriented students can move toward deeper literature engagement, study design, analysis, abstracts, posters, conference presentations, manuscript involvement, graduate-school preparation, and ownership of project components. Students pursuing other paths build transferable skills in teamwork, responsibility, participant interaction, troubleshooting, documentation, communication, and career clarity.

Student feedback has encouraged even more exposure to later research stages, especially data analysis, interpretation, statistics, and manuscript writing. My next mentoring improvements include more analysis mini-lessons, data-to-figure activities, manuscript-development pathways for advanced students, and clearer early explanations of how data collection connects to the eventual scientific product.

title: Research
text:
My research examines how health-promoting behaviors can be designed around the constraints of everyday life, including timing, task demands, individual differences, and the cognitive or practical burden of making healthier choices.
The long-term question is straightforward but scientifically demanding: How can we make healthy behavior actually work in real life? I approach this question as a theory-informed, mechanism-aware, application-driven behavioral scientist.


01


I study whether and how physical activity can be integrated into desk-based work and other everyday settings without unacceptable performance, comfort, or experience tradeoffs.



02


Average effects can conceal meaningful heterogeneity. My work asks when, for whom, and under what conditions an intervention functions as a resource, an added demand, or a neutral option.



03


Health behavior interventions need to support more than one-time choices. I am interested in low-burden intervention delivery, repeated behavior, sustained use, and downstream well-being.

title: Research
text:
Laboratory-To-Field Logic
My program deliberately moves between controlled and applied settings.

Mechanism Feasibility Field effectiveness Sustained use Refined mechanism

This iterative approach lets practical constraints become part of the science rather than a problem discovered only after an intervention leaves the laboratory.

title: Research
text:
Representative Projects


Activity-Permissive Workstations, Performance, and User Experience

Movement integration · task compatibility · user experience

This randomized laboratory study compared sitting, standing, and treadmill walking during desk-based tasks. Findings suggest that treadmill walking can be compatible with some cognitive tasks, while fine-motor interaction may feel more difficult. The broader takeaway is that task-specific compatibility is more useful than asking whether treadmill desks are globally good or bad.
Status: First-author manuscript under review at Applied Ergonomics.


Activity-Permissive Workstations and Acute Social-Evaluative Stress

Stress · psychophysiology · workstation conditions

This preregistered randomized experiment tested whether walking during an acute stressor buffered or compounded stress responses. The preregistered stress-buffering hypothesis was not supported, but walking was not associated with amplified subjective stress and was rated as enjoyable. The study highlights the importance of appropriate physiological baselines when movement itself changes cardiovascular indicators.
Status: First-author manuscript under review at Journal of Occupational Health Psychology.


Dissertation: Timing of Walking Around Acute Stress

Timing · heterogeneity · mixed methods

My dissertation asks whether it matters if a brief walking bout occurs before, during, or after an acute stressor. Current quantitative results do not support a universal stress-regulation benefit of walking timing, while qualitative accounts suggest meaningful heterogeneity in how participants experience walking as preparation, coping, distraction, added demand, or recovery support.
Status: Dissertation proposal passed August 28, 2026; expected Ph.D. completion Summer 2027.


Task-Specific Treadmill-Desk Feasibility

Everyday office tasks · qualitative and mixed-methods work

This mixed-methods line examines which everyday office tasks are compatible with treadmill walking and why. Emerging themes include task demands, ergonomics, social visibility, user control, and pace.
Status: Mixed-methods manuscript development with student mentee involvement.


Longitudinal Treadmill-Desk Field Pilot

Field pilot · daily diary · sustained use

This one-year field pilot follows sustained, self-directed treadmill-desk use among administrative staff. The study is best understood as an intensive longitudinal pilot/case study designed to inform future work on adherence, context, barriers, and person-specific use patterns.


Health Literacy and Menu Labeling

Health literacy · menu labeling · intervention heterogeneity

My published work on health literacy and menu labeling shows that health information interventions do not affect all consumers uniformly. This line is a complementary research domain and a conceptual bridge to the broader question of person-by-intervention fit.

title: Research
text:
Methodological Approach
My work uses randomized experiments, mixed methods, intensive longitudinal and daily-diary field designs, psychophysiological measurement, qualitative interviews, online survey/RCT data, and applied statistical modeling. Across methods, I prioritize feasibility, acceptability, heterogeneity, and translation.

title: Research
text:
Research Trajectory
As an independent faculty member, I plan to build a program on context-sensitive health behavior interventions that reduce the burden of healthy action by fitting movement or other health behaviors into people’s existing tasks, routines, and constraints. Future projects may include task-movement compatibility frameworks, person-by-context moderators of intervention response, and larger field studies using repeated-measures or wearable-supported designs.
